results.blind_working: Amine class depends on how many carbon groups are attached to N, not on the carbon type. In tert-butylamine, N carries one alkyl group and two H atoms, so it is a primary amine.
The parent chain is ethanamine, and the second ethyl group sits on nitrogen. The name is therefore N-ethylethanamine.
The C3H9N amines are propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine, N-methylethanamine and N,N-dimethylmethanamine. That gives 4 isomers.
C6H5CH2NH2 is phenylmethanamine (III). H2N(CH2)6NH2 is hexane-1,6-diamine (IV). C6H5N(CH3)2 is N,N-dimethylbenzenamine (I). p-CH3OC6H4NH2 is p-anisidine (II).

A is true: N is sp3 and the C-N-C angle is about 108°. B is false: in benzylamine N is bonded to CH2, not to the ring, so it is not an aryl amine. C is true: the lone pair delocalises into the ring. D is false: (CH3)4N+Cl- is a quaternary ammonium salt. E is true: class depends on the number of carbons bonded to N. So A, C and E are correct.

In water, dimethylamine is the strongest base. Inductive donation, H-bonded solvation of the cation and steric effects balance best for the 2° amine. Aniline is weakest because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring. NH3 and CH3NH2 lie in between.
For ethyl amines in water, the combined inductive, solvation and steric effects give the order 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3: Et2NH > Et3N > EtNH2 > NH3.

Increasing pKb means decreasing basicity. -OMe (+R) donates more than -CH3 (+I/hyperconjugation), and -NO2 (-R) withdraws. Approximate pKb values: anisidine 8.7 < toluidine 8.9 < aniline 9.4 < p-nitroaniline ~13.
In benzylamine the CH2 group insulates the nitrogen from the ring, so the lone pair is not delocalised. It is therefore more basic than aniline. A is true and R is false.

I: in the gas phase, basicity follows the inductive order 3° > 2°. In water, Me2NH > Me3N because of solvation and steric effects, so I is correct. II: anilinium has pKa about 4.6, methylammonium about 10.6, so anilinium is the stronger acid and II is correct.
The carbylamine (isocyanide) test is given only by primary amines. Aniline is the only primary amine among the options.

A sulphonamide insoluble in aqueous KOH has no acidic N-H, so it comes from a secondary amine. N-methylethanamine is secondary. Tertiary amines do not react at all, and primary amines give alkali-soluble products.
Aromatic primary amines undergo diazotisation at 273-278 K. Benzenediazonium chloride forms and is stable at this temperature, so no N2 is evolved.

A: aliphatic 1° amine gives N2 effervescence (III). B: aniline at low temperature gives a diazonium salt (IV). C: 2° amine gives a yellow oily N-nitrosamine (I). D: N,N-dimethylaniline undergoes ring nitrosation to a green p-nitroso compound (II).

A is true: the N-H of a 1° sulphonamide is acidic. B is false: 3° amines do not react. C is true: p-toluenesulphonyl chloride works in the Hinsberg test. D is true: aniline is a 1° amine. E is false: N-methylaniline is a 2° amine. So A, C and D are correct.
Arenediazonium salts are stable only at low temperature. On warming in aqueous solution they decompose to phenol and N2, so the reaction is kept at 273-278 K.
This is the Balz-Schiemann reaction. HBF4 precipitates the diazonium fluoroborate, and heating that salt gives fluorobenzene plus BF3 and N2.
Bromine water converts aniline to 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Diazotisation followed by H3PO2 replaces the diazonium group with H, leaving 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.
Alkyldiazonium salts are less stable than arenediazonium salts, so A is false. Arenediazonium ions are stabilised by resonance with the ring, so R is true.

I: CuCN/KCN gives PhCN, and LiAlH4 reduces it to PhCH2NH2 (benzylamine), so I is correct. II: coupling with aniline in mildly acidic medium gives yellow p-aminoazobenzene with the -N=N- linkage retained, so II is correct.
